answer: Shrinking the trigger lowers the latency floor, but each micro-batch cycle pays a fixed cost of about 1 second for planning and committing offsets. A 100 ms trigger would spend almost all its time on that overhead, so micro-batch stops paying below about 1 second. Micro-batch latency is trigger plus run time, with p99 near the full trigger plus the slowest run. Near-real-time under about 1 second needs a record-at-a-time engine, which has a 10 to 100 ms floor. Its cost is a second runtime to operate.
